Follow these writing rules. They matter as much as the content:

- Bold used as body emphasis throughout -- reserve bold for a rare callout
- A short rhetorical question with a canned answer -- collapse into one direct statement
- Short buildup, then a reveal: "The best part: it learns." -- state it as a plain sentence
- Emoji or decorative checkmarks in body text -- cut them
- An em dash, section sign or middle dot written as an HTML entity -- write the plain character
- Throat-clearing openers: "needless to say", "at the end of the day" -- state the point directly from the first sentence
- Fake ID tags opening list items: "R-1.", "US-01" -- number the list plainly
- Marketing adjectives: seamless, robust, cutting-edge -- say what is actually true
- The "not just X but Y" construction -- make the point once
- Body paragraphs nearly identical in length -- vary them with what each paragraph has to do
- A significance clause bolted to a sentence: ", underscoring the..." -- delete it, or make it a claim with something behind it
- Three parallel -ing items in a series -- keep the one that carries information
- Fake-humility feedback requests: "would love your feedback on this" -- cut them
- Horizontal rules dropped between sections -- headings already separate sections
- Headings Capitalised Like This -- sentence case
- Vague intensifiers with no number behind them: very, really, quite, significantly -- say how much, or cut the word
- Unnamed authority: "studies show", "experts agree" -- name the actual source, or cut the claim

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write a launch announcement blog post for a new dark mode feature in a note-taking app. Around 250 words.

# Dark mode is here

Dark mode ships today in version 3.2, on iOS, Android, and the web app.

It was the most-requested feature in our feedback tracker for two years running, with 1,840 votes. We put it off longer than we should have, mostly because our editor rendered note content through a theme layer that assumed a white page. Rewriting that layer took four months.

The result is a theme that covers everything, not just the app chrome. Code blocks, tables, inline highlights, math rendering, and the PDF preview all have dark variants that were designed rather than inverted. Images in your notes stay untouched, since dimming them made photos look muddy in testing.

You can set it three ways. Follow the system setting, force it on, or schedule it by time of day. Find these under Settings, then Appearance. If you use the system setting on iOS, the app switches with the OS without a restart.

Two things worth knowing. Our background color is #14161A rather than pure black, because pure black next to white text produces visible halation for many readers. And OLED users who want true black can enable it separately under Appearance, which does save battery on those screens.

We also raised the contrast of the default light theme while we were in there. Body text went from #4A4A4A to #2B2B2B, which brings it to WCAG AA against the page background.

Update from the App Store, Play Store, or reload the web app. The changelog for 3.2 lists the smaller fixes that shipped alongside.

Dark mode ships today in version 3.2, on iOS, Android, and the web app.

It was the most-requested feature in our feedback tracker for two years running, with 1,840 votes. We put it off longer than we should have. Our editor rendered note content through a theme layer that assumed a white page, and rewriting that layer took four months of work that users never see.

The result covers everything, not only the app chrome. Code blocks, tables, inline highlights, math rendering, and the PDF preview all have dark variants that were designed rather than inverted. Images in your notes stay untouched, since dimming them made photos look muddy in testing.

You can set it three ways: follow the system setting, force it on, or schedule it by time of day. Find these under Settings, then Appearance. On iOS, the system setting switches the app with the OS, no restart needed.

Two things worth knowing. Our background color is #14161A rather than pure black, because pure black next to white text produces visible halation for many readers. OLED users who want true black can turn it on separately under Appearance, and it does save battery on those screens.

We also raised the contrast of the default light theme while we were in there. Body text went from #4A4A4A to #2B2B2B, which brings it to WCAG AA against the page background. Nobody asked for that one, but the old value had been bothering us for a while, and the theme rewrite made it a two-line change.

Update from the App Store, Play Store, or reload the web app. The 3.2 changelog lists the smaller fixes that shipped alongside.
